chapters.1.lds: The selected lesson teaches courage in sharing the gospel. Why does Paul explain his visit through mutual encouragement?
chapters.1.summary: Paul opens a letter to the believers in Rome. He calls himself an apostle set apart for God’s good news about his Son. He thanks God that their faith is known in all the world. He has often planned to visit and has been prevented. He says he is not ashamed of the good news. It is God’s power to save the Jew first and also the Greek. God’s wrath, he says, falls on those who trade his glory for images. God gives them up to their desires, and Paul lists the wrongs that follow.
chapters.2.lds: The selected lesson connects inward commitment with conduct. Why does judging another person fail to establish the judge’s innocence?
chapters.2.summary: Paul turns to a person who judges others. He says the judge does the same things and will not escape God’s judgment. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God will repay each one according to works, Jew first and also Greek. There is no partiality with God. Gentiles without the law sometimes do what the law requires. Paul then questions a Jewish teacher of the law who breaks it. He says true circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit.
chapters.3.lds: The selected lesson teaches grace as God’s gift rather than earned salvation. How does one God connect the two peoples in Paul’s argument?
chapters.3.summary: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has and answers that it is great. They were entrusted with God’s words. Still he says Jews and Greeks are all under sin. He quotes a chain of Scriptures: no one is righteous. The law stops every mouth and gives knowledge of sin. Now God’s righteousness comes apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace. Boasting is shut out, and faith upholds the law.
chapters.4.lds: Why does the timing of Abraham’s circumcision matter?
chapters.4.summary: Paul takes Abraham as his example. Scripture says Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. A worker’s pay is owed, but this was counted as a gift. David also calls blessed the one whose sin the Lord does not count. Paul asks when Abraham was counted righteous. It was before he was circumcised. The promise came through faith, so it holds for all his offspring. Abraham trusted God for a son when he was about a hundred years old.
chapters.5.lds: The selected lesson connects grace with changed conduct. Why does Paul stress that Christ died while the recipients remained sinners?
chapters.5.summary: Paul says those justified by faith have peace with God. They rejoice in hope and even in sufferings. Suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still weak. Those once enemies are reconciled through his death. Paul then compares Adam and Christ. Through one man sin and death came to all. Through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.
chapters.6.lds: The selected lesson teaches that grace calls believers toward changed conduct. How does the contrast between wages and gift shape the closing verse?
chapters.6.summary: Paul asks if believers should keep sinning so that grace may grow. He answers that it must never be. Those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death. The old self was crucified with him, and the dead are freed from sin. They are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. Paul asks again if freedom from law permits sin. He says a person is a servant of what he obeys. The wages of sin is death, but God’s free gift is eternal life.
chapters.7.lds: Why does Paul distinguish the command from sin’s use of it?
chapters.7.summary: Paul says the law binds a person only while he lives. A wife is free to marry again when her husband dies. So believers died to the law through Christ’s body and belong to another. Paul asks if the law is sin and denies it. He would not have known coveting without the command not to covet. Sin used the command and brought death. He describes wanting the good and doing the evil he hates. He cries out for rescue and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
chapters.8.lds: The selected lesson teaches becoming like Heavenly Father through Jesus Christ. This is Church teaching. How does the Spirit help when believers cannot supply fitting words?
chapters.8.summary: Paul says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. God sent his Son to do what the law could not. Those led by God’s Spirit are God’s children and call him Abba, Father. They are heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. Creation groans and waits to be set free from decay. Believers groan too and wait in hope. The Spirit helps them pray. Paul says nothing can separate them from God’s love in Christ.
chapters.9.lds: Why does Paul begin with Israel’s gifts and his own grief?
chapters.9.summary: Paul says he has great sorrow for his own people, the Israelites. He lists their gifts, and says Christ came from them by descent. He says God’s word has not failed. Not all descended from Israel are Israel, as Isaac and Jacob show. God told Moses he has mercy on whom he will. Paul answers an objector with the potter and the clay. He quotes Hosea and Isaiah on a people called and a remnant saved. Israel pursued righteousness by works and stumbled over the stone.
chapters.10.lds: The selected lesson connects hearing with growing faith. What must happen before another person can hear and call?
chapters.10.summary: Paul says his prayer for Israel is that they be saved. They have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. He says Christ is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. The word is near, in the mouth and in the heart. Whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Paul asks how people can call on one they have not heard. He quotes Isaiah: not all obeyed, yet God held out his hands all day.
chapters.11.lds: Why must the added branches refuse to boast over the root?
chapters.11.summary: Paul asks if God has rejected his people and says no. He is an Israelite himself, and a remnant remains as in Elijah’s day. Israel’s stumble has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul compares Israel to an olive tree. Some branches were broken off, and wild branches were grafted in. He warns the wild branches not to boast, for they can be cut off. God is able to graft the natural branches in again. Paul says all Israel will be saved and ends with praise.
chapters.12.lds: How do the peace command’s limits affect personal responsibility?
chapters.12.summary: Paul urges the believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. They are not to be shaped by this world but changed by a renewed mind. No one should think too highly of himself. They are one body with many members and different gifts. Paul lists the gifts and then short commands about love. Bless those who persecute you. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Leave revenge to God, feed a hungry enemy, and overcome evil with good.
chapters.13.lds: The selected lesson teaches that love fulfills God’s commands. How does love explain the listed commands through preventing harm?
chapters.13.summary: Paul tells every person to be subject to the governing authorities. He says they are appointed by God and carry the sword against wrongdoing. Believers should pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor where owed. They should owe nothing except love for one another. Love of neighbor sums up the commands against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting. Paul says the night is nearly over and the day is near. They should put away deeds of darkness. They should put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
chapters.14.lds: The selected lesson warns against judging others through differences in practice. How can using freedom damage the person one should welcome?
chapters.14.summary: Paul tells the believers to accept one who is weak in faith. One eats everything, and another eats only vegetables. One honors a certain day, and another treats all days alike. Each does it for the Lord and will answer to God. So they must stop judging one another. Paul says nothing is unclean in itself. Yet they must not grieve a brother by what they eat. God’s kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
chapters.15.lds: The selected lesson connects Scripture with faith and hope. How does the Jerusalem gift make the relationship between peoples practical?
chapters.15.summary: Paul says the strong should bear the weaknesses of the weak. Christ did not please himself. Paul tells them to accept one another as Christ accepted them. He quotes four Scriptures about Gentiles praising God. He explains that he has taught from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. He plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain. First he will carry a gift from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem’s poor. He asks them to pray for his safety in Judea.
chapters.16.lds: Why does Paul ask for Phoebe’s welcome before the other greetings?
chapters.16.summary: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the assembly at Cenchreae. He asks the Romans to receive her and help her. He greets Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for him. He greets many others by name, among them Mary, Andronicus, Junia, and Rufus. He warns against those who cause divisions. Timothy and others send greetings. Tertius, who wrote the letter down, adds his own. The letter ends with a blessing.
